images.alt: A beige Commodore 128 home computer with a full-width keyboard and numeric keypad, photographed from above
images.caption: The Commodore 128, wider than a C64 to hold a full numeric keypad and function keys, and three computers in one case.

images.alt: A Commodore 128 computer on display in a computer museum
images.caption: Designed against a punishing schedule by a small hardware team led by Bil Herd, in time for the January 1985 Consumer Electronics Show.

images.alt: Close view of a Commodore 128 keyboard and case, showing the function keys and Commodore badge
images.caption: The 128 had to be a Commodore 64 as well as its own machine: the C64 was still the best-selling computer in the world, and nothing could be allowed to break it.

images.commonsFile: File:Commodore 128 set-up with a 1541, 1571, 1200 baud Modem, and two displays (filtered).jpg
images.alt: A Commodore 128 computer connected to two external disk drives, a modem, and two monitors
images.caption: The 1571 drive could read the actual MFM disk formats other CP/M machines wrote, so a home computer bought for games could read an office's floppies.

images.alt: A Commodore 128 computer with its monitor displaying a CP/M boot sequence and command prompt
images.caption: Press the exhibit's CP/M button and the Z80 takes the bus: this is the operating system that ran the office before MS-DOS did.
